title: Attention Sinks Induce Gradient Sinks: Massive Activations as Gradient Regulators in Transformers
claim: A standard pre-norm block's forward and backward paths, with the measured gradient quantities and the point where our modification is inserted.
layout: 3 panels: forward and backward stacked left, attention detail right; dashed dividers
description: A three-panel architecture diagram on a white background. Panel (a), top left, shows the forward pass of a pre-norm Transformer block. A residual line runs left to right from h^l to h^{l+1/2} to h^{l+1}. Each sublayer branch has an RMSNorm box (purple) followed by an Attention or MLP (SwiGLU) box (green), and each rejoins the residual at a plus node. Panel (b), bottom left, shows the backward flow with orange dotted arrows. Gradients g1, g2 and g3 are colored red, green and blue and combine as g1+g3. A gray box defines the Bloat, Compress and Change ratios. Panel (c), right, expands attention. Q, K and V stacks feed RoPE and Scaled Dot-Product Attention. A red V-scale box sits on the V path, and circled markers 1 and 2 label the baseline and V-scale alternatives. A green line links panel (a)'s attention box to panel (c).
caption: Pre-norm Transformer architecture, gradient measurements, and V-scale placement. (a) Forward computation through the attention and MLP sublayers. (b) Backward flow and gradient measurements for the attention sublayer. Detailed definitions are given in Section [ref]. (c) Expanded attention computation. Value paths 1 and 2 are alternatives for the baseline model and the V-scale variant proposed in Section [ref], respectively.
abstract: Attention sinks and massive activations are recurring and closely related phenomena in Transformer models. Existing explanations have largely focused on the forward pass, yet in pre-norm Transformers, large residual-stream norms play only an indirect forward role because sublayers operate on normalized inputs. We study this relationship from the perspective of backpropagation. Empirically and theoretically, we show that under causal masking, attention sinks can induce pronounced gradient concentration, which we term gradient sinks. Since the RMSNorm Jacobian attenuates gradients roughly in inverse proportion to input norm, massive activations can be understood as adaptive regulators of this localized gradient pressure during training. This interpretation predicts that attenuating sink-induced gradients should weaken massive activations. We test this prediction with V-scale, a modification that adjusts backpropagated gradients on the value paths. In V-scale models and a backward-only control, attention sinks are preserved, whereas massive activations are suppressed. These results identify gradient sinks as a backward-pass counterpart of attention sinks, and massive activations as an adaptive RMSNorm-mediated response that attenuates the resulting localized training pressure. Our code is available at https://github.com/LARS-research/GradientSink.
